articles.title: England begin ODI tri-series with Pakistan and Sri Lanka as Henry Crocombe, Sam Curran and spinners look to impress
articles.summary: Success in the subcontinent could help players push for Test places in South Africa; Mason Crane hoping for first England appearance in over eight years; watch Harry Brook's side's first game, against Pakistan, live on Sky Sports from 8.30am Tuesday (9am first ball)
articles.body:
Having completed an ODI series victory over Sri Lanka on September 27, they return to that format in the subcontinent from Tuesday as they take on Pakistan in Rawalpindi - live on Sky Sports (9am first ball) - in a tri-series that also includes Sri Lanka.

It marks the start of a packed winter schedule that goes on to feature a white-ball tour of Australia, Test trips to South Africa and Bangladesh and then a return to Australia for the pink-ball, 150th-anniversary Test match in March.

Here we look at the questions for England in this tri-series and what knock-on effects they could have for the Test challenges to come…

Will spinners press claims for Test call-ups?

When it comes to spin bowling in white-ball cricket, England have struck on a decent formula. Adil Rashid as the main man - something he has been for well over a decade now - supported by a number of all-rounders, including Will Jacks and Liam Dawson.

In Test cricket, though, spin is a real issue. Dan Lawrence is the first-choice option for now, principally because of his batting prowess, and while Shoaib Bashir has received another central contract, he has only played two Tests in the last year.

So, this white-ball series in the subcontinent offers the chance for England's younger spinners - Jacks, James Coles and the recalled Mason Crane - to push for squad places on the Test tour of South Africa from December 17, also live on Sky Sports.

Jacks, who played in four Ashes Tests last winter, and Coles could appeal because they, like Lawrence, bring much with the bat. Crane is the only out-and-out bowler in that trio but has advanced his batting with two Championship tons for Glamorgan last term.

At the very least, Crane, in line for his first England appearance since 2018, will be keen to prove he should be Rashid's leg-spin back-up in ODI cricket and perhaps his long-term successor, too, having leapfrogged Rehan Ahmed in the white-ball pecking order.

Will we see what the fuss is about with Crocombe?

Seam bowler Henry Crocombe was awarded a two-year central contact last week despite not yet having made a senior appearance for his country. That shows the regard England hold him in and you sense he will be unleased sooner or later.

The 25-year-old, who will join Surrey from Sussex ahead of the 2027 domestic season, has enjoyed most success in red-ball cricket to date, with his 125 wickets in 51 matches including back-to-back hat-tricks against Somerset and Essex this campaign.

Crocombe's 50-over stats are not too shabby, though - 49 wickets in 36 matches - and the length of his central contract would suggest England view him as a multi-format bowler, alongside Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson.

The Eastbourne-born quick is set to make his T20I debut in Australia in November, while he must have an excellent shout of making that Test trip to South Africa as well.

Another talking point from England's updated central-contract list last week was Ben Duckett missing out on a two-year extension. The batter's deal runs until 2027 so he probably shouldn't be fretting about his spot too much, although he could do with some runs.

To be fair, the 31-year-old has scored runs in ODIs since a lean time in that format towards the end of 2025 when he registered a top-score of 31 at home to South Africa and then managed only 11 in three games away to New Zealand.

But with Jacob Bethell soon to return from injury and Tom Banton having just hit his maiden ODI hundred, perhaps Duckett's opening berth is not quite as secure as it was.

If the Nottinghamshire man endures a tough time in this tri-series and then in the one-day internationals in Australia next month, chat will inevitably turn to the surety of his Test place, too.

Duckett is averaging only 23.42 across his last 11 Tests with a solitary hundred and a second-highest score of 42. His name has not really been mentioned when it comes to who will drop out of the XI when Bethell is back. He will want to keep it that way...

Will Curran audition to be the new Stokes?

Sam Curran has not played a Test match in over five years, mainly because England had Ben Stokes fulfilling the pace-bowling all-rounder job but with Stokes bowing out from international cricket this summer, in typically eye-catching style, there is a spot available.

Curran would probably have been involved in the 3-0 red-ball rout of Pakistan if not for a groin injury ending his home summer early and he has surely been earmarked for a place in South Africa this winter, in the squad at least, if not the XI.

England don't need a reminder of the Surrey player's talent before he returns to the Test arena - he is whip-smart and tenacious, has variations with the ball and class with the bat, and having captained domestically, would add much-needed leadership to the group.

It's probably just a case of where his body is at after that injury.

If you rewind to around this time last year, when England were whumped 3-0 in New Zealand, we were beginning to wonder whether the 2019 World Cup winners would have to go through the ignominy of a qualifying tournament to reach the 2027 edition in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, such was their lowly ranking.

However, back-to-back series wins in Sri Lanka and at home to India - Harry Brook's side coming from behind to win both of those assignments - assuaged any fears and they then made it three ODI series victories on the trot when they beat - no, thrashed - Sri Lanka in a decider at The Kia Oval last month.

England will be expected to make the tri-series final as the teams ranked fifth (Pakistan), sixth (England) and seventh (Sri Lanka) meet over the next week and a bit, especially with their 50-over success against Sri Lanka already this year.

They should face a stronger Pakistan than the one they crushed in the Test arena this summer - the tri-series hosts started with a victory over Sri Lanka and have won their last three bilateral ODI series at home, including against Australia and South Africa.

If England can continue their 50-over resurgence here, it will only add to the notion that they could be genuine contenders at the 2017 World Cup, a competition they were once scrambling to qualify for.

articles.title: Ranji Trophy: Chinmay Sutar creates history with unbeaten 400, becomes only second Indian to reach the milestone
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Mumbai batter Chinmay Sutar made history on Monday when, playing only his second first-class fixture, the 29-year-old slammed 400 not out, in an
articles.body: MUMBAI: Mumbai batter Chinmay Sutar made history on Monday when, playing only his second first-class fixture, the 29-year-old slammed 400 not out, in an marathon innings spanning 517 balls and studded with 46 fours and seven sixes, in a Ranji Trophy Plate group match between Mizoram and Nagaland at the Nagaland Cricket Stadium in Sovima.During his epic knock, Sutar, who played one match (against Maharashtra) in the Vijay Hazare Trophy for Mumbai last season, went past Prithvi Shaw's 379 to record the second-highest score in the history of the Ranji Trophy, and joined BB Nimbalkar, who had scored 443 not out for Maharashtra against Kathiawar in 1948-49 to become only the second Indian batsman to score 400 in a first-class match, and the 10th overall.Sutar was within touching distance for the all-time record for the Ranji Trophy's highest-ever individual score, held by BB Nimbalkar, Unbeaten on 392 at tea, Sutar reached 400 in the 155th over, with Mizoram declaring the innings at 581 for nine immediately after the No. 3 bat reached the special milestone.Sutar put on an unbeaten 190-run partnership for the tenth wicket with Lalrempunia Chhakchhuak, who made 14 not out off 76 balls.Such was the impact of Sutar's knock that the second highest score in Mizoram's innings was Jehu Anderson (69).Riding on Sutar's colossal knock, Mizoram made 581 for nine declared. Sutar had fallen run out on 99 on his first-class debut in the previous round against Manipur at Nadiad.Chinmay's father Rajesh Sutar is a former Mumbai off-spinning allrounder who once opened the batting with the legendary Sachin Tendulkar for Mumbai. He played seven first-class matches.Chinmay Sutar played for the India Under-23 team in the 2019 ACC Emerging Teams Asia Cup in Bangladesh.Sutar has been one of the top run-getters in the past two seasons of T20 Mumbai, thus playing a stellar role in Maratha Royals’ back-to-back title wins in this period.Sutar scored half-centuries-62 off 49 balls & 61 off 52 balls for Maratha Royals in the semis and finals of the 2026 T20 Mumbai League, eventually finishing with 210 runs.In 2025, he was the ‘Orange Cap’ winner in the T20 Mumbai League.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: Pragyan Ojha will take over as chairman of the BCCI’s Men’s Selection Committee following Ajit Agarkar’s exit, while former India spinner Ramesh Powar has
articles.body: Pragyan Ojha will take over as chairman of the BCCI’s Men’s Selection Committee following Ajit Agarkar’s exit, while former India spinner Ramesh Powar has been appointed as a new member of the five-member panel, marking a change in the composition of the team responsible for selecting India’s senior men’s side.The Cricket Advisory Committee (CAC), comprising Ashok Malhotra and Jatin Paranjape, conducted interviews at the BCCI headquarters before unanimously recommending Powar’s appointment. Ojha will chair the committee based on seniority, determined by the number of Test matches played.The new selection committee comprises Pragyan Ojha (chairperson), Shiv Sundar Das, RP Singh, Ajay Ratra and Ramesh Powar.Agarkar’s tenure ends after major ICC triumphsAgarkar, who was appointed chairman in July 2023, completed his tenure on October 4, 2026, after deciding not to seek an extension. During his stint, India won the 2024 and 2026 T20 World Cups and the 2025 Champions Trophy, while also claiming two Asia Cup titles and back-to-back Asian Games gold medals.The BCCI acknowledged Agarkar’s commitment and contribution, crediting the selection committee with overseeing a successful period for Indian cricket.Ojha joined panel in September 2025Ojha was inducted into the Men’s Selection Committee at the BCCI’s 94th Annual General Meeting in September 2025, alongside former India pacer RP Singh. He now takes over the chairperson’s role after serving on the panel for just over a year.The former left-arm spinner represented India in 24 Tests, 18 ODIs and six T20Is. His Test experience places him ahead of the other members of the current panel under the BCCI’s seniority criterion.Powar, meanwhile, brings both international playing experience and a substantial coaching background to the committee. He represented India in two Tests and 31 ODIs and has served as head coach of the India women’s team, Mumbai and Gujarat, besides working as bowling coach at the BCCI Centre of Excellence.During his stint with the India women’s team, Powar guided the side to an Asia Cup title and a silver medal at the Commonwealth Games.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Harry Brook: England captain says he has 'learned a lot' from off-field issues
articles.summary: White-ball captain Harry Brook says he has "learned a lot" as a captain and a person - and wants to be the player England fans rely on.
articles.body:
White-ball captain Harry Brook says he has "learned a lot" as a captain and a person - and wants to be the player England fans rely on.

It is almost a year since Brook, 27, was punched by a nightclub bouncer on the eve of a match against New Zealand in Wellington, which led to doubts over his future as skipper.

He has not made a Test hundred since, including failing to do so during last winter's Ashes, but has been in excellent white-ball form and has overseen a resurgence in England's 50-over and T20 sides.

"I've learnt a lot as a captain, I've learnt a lot as a person," Brook, whose side return to action in a 50-over tri-series on Tuesday, told Press Association.

"I know it wasn't an ideal situation to put myself in, but I feel like as a captain and a leader I've learnt a lot.

"Responsibilities and leadership aren't just on the field, they're more so off the field as well and actions speak louder than words."

How one rule change is altering the face of one-day cricket

Brook remains one of England's most fascinating cricketers.

Despite being white-ball skipper and serving as Test vice-captain, he was overlooked for the red-ball job when Ben Stokes retired, with Joe Root preferred.

He averages a formidable 53.08 in Tests - the highest for England in almost 60 years - with 10 centuries, but often draws criticism for his aggressive, some say reckless, batting.

While he has failed to convert any of his seven fifties into centuries since the Ashes, he still averages 41.57 and has scored hundreds as captain in T20s and one-day internationals in that time.

"I enjoy the extra responsibility," he said. "I like the extra little bit of added pressure.

"I'm not going to go out there and score runs every time I bat but I want to be the man that is in that match-winning situation who can get us over the line.

"I know there have been a few innings where I haven't managed to do that but hopefully I've turned that corner and I can really be the man England fans and the team rely on."

The debate around Brook was perhaps best summed up by Stokes telling the Yorkshireman he is talented enough to average 65 or 70.

"Personally I'm not that bothered about the stats, I've always said I think there should be a match-winning column in your stats – that's not there," Brook said.

"I write stuff down and I try and judge myself on whether I've had a match-winning performance or match-winning impact in that specific game and I try and tally it up at the end of the year and see how well I've done."

His 50-over side play Pakistan in Rawalpindi on Tuesday (09:00 BST) in their first match of a tri-series that also includes Sri Lanka. The hosts beat Sri Lanka in the series opener on Sunday.

After struggling in the format since their dismal World Cup defence in 2023, England have won three ODI series in a row this year as they build towards next year's World Cup.

Wicketkeeper Jos Buttler is injured for this series while fast bowler Jofra Archer has been rested. England resisted naming their team 24 hours early and will instead do so at the toss.

"In the last six to eight months we're certainly trending in the right direction as a squad," Brook said.

"We're really building towards the make-up of the side that we want.

"Me and Baz [head coach Brendon McCullum] feel like we've got a squad where if someone does go down five minutes before the toss, we're in a position where someone else can come in and fill that role perfectly well."

articles.title: Ranji Trophy: Sachin Yadav, Karan Lamba miss double tons by six runs each after 338-run stand
articles.summary: JAIPUR: If Day One was about building a foundation, Day Two turned into a relentless exhibition of dominance by Sachin Yadav and Karan Lamba that ended in
articles.body: JAIPUR: If Day One was about building a foundation, Day Two turned into a relentless exhibition of dominance by Sachin Yadav and Karan Lamba that ended in uncanny heartbreak. In a rare cricketing coincidence, both batters missed out on coveted double centuries, falling agonizingly six runs short of the landmark on identical scores of 194 in Rajasthan's Group ‘D’ Ranji Trophy fixture against Railways at the Sawai Man Singh Stadium here on Monday.Resuming from the overnight score of 247/2, the Rajasthan duo continued to dictate terms before Sachin’s dismissal sparked a post-lunch collapse as the hosts eventually folded for 497 all out.The final session belonged to the hosts’ bowlers. Debutant pacer Danish Bhambu impressed with his disciplined line and length, finding good support from Chetan Sharma and left-arm seamer Akash Singh.On a pitch that was still playing well, the seam trio did an excellent job of squeezing the run flow. However, it was left-arm spinner Mohit Changra who provided the hosts with their first breakthrough, trapping opener Vivek Singh lbw.At stumps, Railways were 46/1, trailing by 451 runs.Earlier, Karan, playing his 11th First-Class game, completed his third Ranji hundred in no time, ensuring another long day for the Railways’ bowlers. The sheer scale of the dominance even sparked some tongue-in-cheek chatter in the visiting dressing room. With the scoreboard ticking away relentlessly, a few in their camp jokingly muttered, "Yeh kya pitch banwaya hai (what kind of a wicket has been readied)?"Reflecting on the surface, Karan noted, "You rarely get wickets like this in domestic cricket. The pitch was favoring batting. I tried to stay put and play a long innings."The morning session brought its own test when the new ball was introduced, making life tricky for the batters. Edges flew, but Railways were let down by poor fielding as a couple of catches went down. Weathering the storm, Sachin and Karan expertly defended and left the probing deliveries.Once the early threat wore off, they unleashed their strokes. Sachin compiled his 194 off 358 balls with 22 fours and four sixes, while Karan matched him brick-for-brick with a 194 off 284 deliveries, laced with 19 fours and 2 sixes.Having trained together for years at the Rajiv Gandhi Cricket Academy, the duo’s deep understanding was evident on the field as they shared a partnership of 338 runs. "We know each other's strengths," Karan shared. "Our communication was very easy because we have played cricket together for years."Together, their marathon alliance completely broke the back of the Railways attack. Sachin was eventually stumped, while Karan holed out at point. articles.title: South Africa vs Australia: Hosts' batting issues exposed again as Scott Boland takes four
articles.summary: Australia expose South Africa's batting frailties again as Scott Boland takes four wickets to leave hosts in trouble in second Test.
articles.body:
South Africa 97-5: Bavuma 41*; Boland 4-31

For much of Monday it appeared rain would deny any meaningful play taking place on day two of the second Test between South Africa and Australia.

In the end, the hosts may have wished that remained the case as their top-order frailties were exposed once again in Gqeberha.

With the Proteas 97-5 at the close, the balance of power in the series remains firmly with Australia.

It took Australia's metronome Scott Boland only seven deliveries to add to his two wickets taken amid the rain on day one.

Relentless in his line and lengths, the 37-year-old found the perfect length to drag debutant Marques Ackerman onto the front foot.

Ackerman defended nicely for 38 balls but here he neither defended nor unleashed a drive.

Instead, he stumbled forward and became the 85th victim of Boland's 20-Test career as he nicked through to wicketkeeper Alex Carey.

Boland ended the day with 4-31 as he, once again, emphatically pushed his case.

That Ackerman, one of two batting changes from their first-Test defeat, was opening the batting against the red ball for the first time in his career pointed to the issues South Africa face.

The other new face, Matthew Breetzke, was brought in on the back of his white-ball form after Tristan Stubbs played two poor strokes in the first Test.

Breetzke's feet barely moved in making four from 17. He was eventually dismissed trying to force Mitchell Starc loosely through the covers off the back foot.

A result of Ackerman's selection was Ryan Rickelton, another fine white-ball player with a modest red-ball record, being moved from opener to number six and wicketkeeper.

After top-edging a pull last week, he was worked over by Pat Cummins' bouncers late on day two.

He had already been hit on the body and dropped on 26 by Marnus Labuschagne when, stuck on the crease, he edged Boland while pushing tentatively outside off stump.

On another day the ball would have found the turf but Matt Renshaw stuck out a right hand at first slip and somehow scooped the ball up above the ground.

Boland's Test bowling average now stands at 18.08. No bowler since the First World War has taken as many wickets at a better rate.

His probing has ensured Australia have not missed spinner Nathan Lyon, who he replaced, or Josh Hazlewood, who remained at the team hotel throughout the day because of illness.

Of Boland's 84 deliveries across this innings, 63% of his deliveries were on a good line and length, while 24% of those would have gone on to hit the stumps.

On the latter metric, Cummins has the next best record but lags behind at 12%.

Whether Boland has proven yet again he is ideal for seaming conditions or that he is deserving of more more opportunities can be debated. Ollie Robinson, who bowls a similar style, will surely have taken note as he prepares for England's tour of South Africa back home.

With the weather set to improve, the Proteas have three days remaining in this Test to reverse the momentum of the series which only appears to be heading in one direction.

Much will depend on Temba Bavuma, who remained on 41 not out, and seamer Kagiso Rabada.

Rabada returned match figures of 11-150 against Australia on this ground in 2018 - a South Africa win which levelled that four-match series going into the infamous Sandpaper Test.

The hosts may need similar and more here because right now their batting does not appear up to the test.

articles.title: South Africa vs Australia: Scott Boland takes fourth wicket late on rain-hit second day of second Test in Gqeberha
articles.summary: First two sessions of second day in Gqeberha washed out; Scott Boland has 4-31, including Ryan Rickelton to stunning Matt Renshaw catch late on as South Africa close on 97-5; watch day three of second Test, live on Sky Sports+ from 8.30am, Tuesday (play starts 9am)
articles.body:
After rain washed out the first two sessions of the second day, when South Africa's first innings finally resumed at 20-2 they swiftly lost a third wicket after only a couple of overs.

Boland (4-31), who had taken two wickets with consecutive deliveries on day one, added debutant Marques Ackerman caught behind for six.

Mitchell Starc (1-27) then struck to remove Matthew Breetzke (4) - also nicking off, when chasing a wide drive - to have the Proteas rocking at 40-4.

Australia were shorn of one of their four-pronged front-line pace options, with Josh Hazlewood absent on day two due to illness. He is expected to be available for the remainder of the Test.

South Africa gradually grew into proceedings, their captain Temba Bavuma leading from the front with an unbeaten 41 as part of a fifty partnership for the fifth wicket with Rickelton.

But, just as the pair would have been preparing to put their feet up for the evening and resume battle in the morning, Rickelton - dropped on 26 by Marnus Labuschagne - became Boland's latest victim as Matt Renshaw claimed a sensational, one-handed catch low to his right at slip.

South Africa are the reigning world Test champions, having beaten current table-toppers Australia in the 2025 final, but they trail 1-0 in this three-match series after a heavy 214-run defeat in the first Test.

articles.title: Stephen Fleming suggests England coach should be English
articles.summary: New Zealander Stephen Fleming, England’s new Test coach, suggests the national team should be led by someone from England.
articles.body:
New Zealander Stephen Fleming, England's new Test coach, has suggested the national team should be led by someone from England.

Fleming, who will take charge of his first series in South Africa in December, is the latest overseas coach to lead the England men's team.

Since 1999, only two Englishmen - Peter Moores (twice) and Chris Silverwood - have been in charge of the Test side, while Ashley Giles had a spell as white-ball coach.

In the same time period England have been led by two Zimbabweans, in Duncan Fletcher and Andy Flower, and Australian Trevor Bayliss - while Fleming has succeeded his fellow Kiwi Brendon McCullum, who remains white-ball coach. Another Australian, Matthew Mott, also had time in charge of the white-ball team.

Fleming's backroom team, announced last week, is heavily weighted towards homegrown coaches.

Former England opener Marcus Trescothick, who was in interim charge of the Test team earlier this year, is joined by ex-England wicketkeeper James Foster and former spinner Richard Dawson.

Jonathan Trott, an Ashes winner with England, is about to begin a spell in charge of England Lions. Both Trott and Dawson were in the running for the Test job before Fleming was appointed.

Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, former New Zealand captain Fleming said it will be a "priority" of his tenure to help develop English coaches.

"I do believe that primarily the national team should be coached by a national representative," said Fleming.

"I'm grateful for the opportunity, but there will be some development in terms of the coaching, and you can see by our staff."

As well as Fleming and McCullum filling the head coach roles for the men's national teams, England's selector, Marcus North, is Australian.

In September it was announced that another Australian, Leah Poulton, will become the managing director of England women. Between 2020 and 2023 England women's head coach was Lisa Keightley, the former Australia international.

In addition to developing the coaches on his own staff, Fleming said he will also occasionally invite county coaches and former England players into the set-up.

"There are some really key people who have come back into the system and I'm really pleased about that," he said.

"I look forward to working with them, but it is a real focus and it's an ambition as well that you will also get county coaches who will be introduced at certain times and you will get past players that will be asked to come back as well.

"It's really inclusive and a comfortable nature of using what's around, but also driving what should be driven within the county game and the English game."

Listen to the full interview with Stephen Fleming on the TMS podcast

One of the criticisms of McCullum's four-year spell in charge of the Test team was his lack of time spent around the county game.

In September, Fleming visited some counties and also spoke of his affection for the domestic game in England. The former batter had spells as a player with Nottinghamshire, Yorkshire and Middlesex.

He confirmed he will spend part of next summer watching county cricket in the build-up to the home Ashes series.

"Yep, I'll be around and I really enjoyed this year getting to catch up," said Fleming. "A lot of the guys I played with are now in positions either coaching or the head positions at counties.

"It was good to catch up with those guys and get a feel for where the county game is at. I really enjoyed it and it will be a key part to continuing developing players."

Fleming was appointed in July, though did not take charge for the series against Pakistan in August and September, meaning his first series at the helm will be the three matches in South Africa in December and January.

The squad for that series is due to be named in the first week of November.

England did not pick a specialist spinner in any of the three Tests against Pakistan, instead fielding four frontline seamers.

In South Africa's ongoing Test against Australia in Gqeberha, the tourists have omitted Nathan Lyon despite the off-spinner sitting sixth on the all-time list of Test wicket-takers with 573.

Last week, Shoaib Bashir was named as the only specialist red-ball spinner on England's list of fully centrally contracted players, while Mason Crane and Liam Patterson-White were given development deals.

Following the tour of South Africa, spin will play a big role on the two-Test tour of Bangladesh in February.

Asked if Bashir's contract means he is England's number-one spinner, Fleming said the Derbyshire man represents "continuity".

"I acknowledge there's a raft of spinners just below that, that at times are putting their hand up," said Fleming.

"There is a raft of spinners there and are probably looking for an opportunity, and finding those conditions, it could be Bangladesh, where there could be two or three that will come along.

"The team could look quite different and that's the horses for courses example.

"But Bashir has got some experience and is still very young. There's an aspect of still looking and developing, and trying to find that right combination in the spin department."

articles.title: ‘Give Vaibhav Sooryavanshi harsh truth’: Ex-India cricketer explains Gautam Gambhir, management’s approach
articles.summary: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s continued absence from India’s playing XI has left fans frustrated, but former India spinner Murali Kartik believes there is little
articles.body: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s continued absence from India’s playing XI has left fans frustrated, but former India spinner Murali Kartik believes there is little reason for the team management to rush the 15-year-old into the side when the established opening options are performing well.Despite being named Player of the Series during India’s tour of Zimbabwe, Sooryavanshi did not feature in the subsequent T20I series against Afghanistan and West Indies. The teenage batter is also yet to make his senior India debut on home soil, even as his performances in the IPL have made him one of the country’s most talked-about young talents.His absence has become a talking point at India’s home matches, with supporters hoping to see him play. Sooryavanshi did get an opportunity to open alongside Abhishek Sharma during the Asian Games, offering a glimpse of his potential, but his wait for a regular spot in the senior team’s playing XI continues.Speaking in an interaction facilitated by Sony Sports Network, Kartik backed the management’s decision to retain its existing opening combination, highlighting the contributions of Sanju Samson and Abhishek. He also pointed to the presence of Ishan Kishan, whose recent form has made competition for a place at the top of the order even tougher."I am not somebody who makes a change for the sake of it. I know change is constant, but change for the right reasons. There has to be a reason why there is a change. So, when it comes to the opening duo in India, I know they are a bit inconsistent, but that is what has won games for you," said Karthik.Samson and Abhishek have accumulated 1,125 runs together in 38 T20Is, making them India’s fourth-highest run-scoring partnership in the format. Kartik believes their record, combined with the quality of the other available batters, makes it difficult to justify a change simply to accommodate another promising player."We have seen the quality of Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma, both of them are sitting right up there. Then you've got Ishan Kishan, who's your number two, number one players out there, so it's very difficult to make the change."Kartik draws comparison with Yashasvi JaiswalKartik also compared Sooryavanshi’s situation with that of Yashasvi Jaiswal, who has found opportunities limited in India’s white-ball setup despite producing impressive performances in Test cricket and the IPL.With Rohit Sharma and Shubman Gill established at the top of the order in ODIs, Jaiswal has had to wait for his chance in the format. Kartik sees a similar challenge for Sooryavanshi, whose talent is not in question but who must contend with players already occupying the positions he is targeting."Yes, we get excited because he's an exciting talent. We are not taking anything away, but at the end of the day, it's like Yashasvi Jaiswal in white-ball cricket. Do you make the change just for the sake of it, just to knock somebody off?""I don't think I am in favor of that. I've never been in favor of that. I don't think going forward I'll ever be in favor of that," said Karthik.The former spinner stressed that a player’s ability alone does not automatically justify a change in the playing XI. In his view, selection decisions must be based on a clear need rather than the excitement surrounding a young prospect.‘You have to wait for your opportunity’Kartik acknowledged that Sooryavanshi’s opportunity could come if one of the established batters goes through a prolonged lean patch. The youngster made his India debut in England when Samson was struggling for runs, illustrating how changes in form can open doors for players waiting on the sidelines.However, Kartik said there was no way to predict when such a situation might arise. Until then, Sooryavanshi must remain prepared to step in whenever the team needs him.At the end of the day, we can't predict what's going to happen. Tomorrow, it could be that one of the batters going 15 innings without getting runs, and you are forced to make a change."So, at that point of time, you want the second guy who's waiting. The guy waiting behind the door, ready to come out and say, 'listen, I'm there.'""And that's exactly how it should be handled, rather than saying, oh, we like him, people want to see him, so let's bring him in. No, that's being unfair on the guys who are already there," said Karthik.Beyond selection, Kartik believes it is important for the team management to be honest with Sooryavanshi about his position in the squad. He pointed to the messages from head coach Gautam Gambhir and captain Shreyas Iyer, who have stressed that the youngster must remain patient and consistent with his preparation.Kartik said that while hearing such a message might be difficult for a player eager to prove himself, being told the truth is better than being left uncertain about his future."Even if you have to give them the harsh truth, it's better to give it to them, because you take it on your chin. You might not like it; it's not palatable for a while, but it is what it is. You have to deal with it and move on.""I think that is the best way to go about things. Because Shreyas has spoken about it, Gautam has spoken about it, I'm pretty sure they're having the right word with Sooryavanshi, because he's there. Nobody is saying that he's not there. articles.summary: MUMBAI: Former India off-spinner Ramesh Powar was appointed to the men’s selection committee on Monday, with former India left-arm spinner Pragyan Ojha
articles.body: MUMBAI: Former India off-spinner Ramesh Powar was appointed to the men’s selection committee on Monday, with former India left-arm spinner Pragyan Ojha taking over as its chairperson. Powar replaces former India pacer Ajit Agarkar, who headed the panel.Ojha, who played 24 Tests, will lead the committee on the basis of seniority. He had already been serving as interim chairman when squads across formats were picked for the upcoming New Zealand tour. According to a BCCI source, Ojha left for New Zealand with the Indian team on Monday for the tour, which comprises five T20Is, five ODIs and two Tests.Powar was selected unanimously by the BCCI’s two-member Cricket Advisory Committee (CAC), comprising former India cricketers Ashok Malhotra and Jatin Paranjape, after interviews with seven candidates at the board’s headquarters here.The CAC also interviewed candidates for five positions on the junior selection committee. “We will announce the new junior selection committee in a day or two,” BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia told TOI.Ojha has been a member of the senior selection committee since Sept 2025, alongside Shiv Sunder Das, RP Singh and Ajay Ratra. articles.title: Who is Ben Treloar? Australian umpire set to officiate in Ranji Trophy
articles.summary: Australian umpire Ben Treloar will officiate in two Ranji Trophy matches in India, while Indian umpire Parashar Joshi will travel to Australia to
articles.body: Australian umpire Ben Treloar will officiate in two Ranji Trophy matches in India, while Indian umpire Parashar Joshi will travel to Australia to officiate in two Sheffield Shield matches and one One Day Cup game as part of the CA-BCCI Umpire Exchange Program.The program will give both umpires an opportunity to gain experience by officiating in domestic cricket competitions in each other's countries.Ben Treloar to officiate in two Ranji Trophy matchesTreloar has officiated in 30 first-class matches, 20 List A matches and 39 Big Bash League games. He has also worked in two Women's One Day Internationals and four Women's T20 Internationals.Apart from his work as an umpire, Treloar serves as Cricket New South Wales' Umpire Education Officer. He helps train and develop future match officials.His work in umpire education has earned him four George Borwick Memorial Awards from the New South Wales Cricket Umpires and Scorers Association.Treloar will begin his India assignment with Delhi's Ranji Trophy match against Gujarat from October 18 to 21 in Delhi. He will then officiate in Mumbai's match against Haryana from October 26 to 29 in Mumbai.Parashar Joshi to officiate in AustraliaJoshi has experience across several Indian domestic cricket competitions. He has officiated in 19 first-class matches in the Ranji Trophy and Duleep Trophy, 32 List A matches in the Vijay Hazare Trophy and Deodhar Trophy, and 40 T20 matches.His T20 assignments include matches in the Indian Premier League and the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy.Joshi's Australian assignment will begin with Queensland's Sheffield Shield match against Tasmania at the Gabba from November 11 to 14.He will then officiate in the One Day Cup match between the two teams at the same venue on November 16.His exchange program will conclude with the Sheffield Shield match between New South Wales and Queensland at the Sydney Cricket Ground from November 22 to 25.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
